description: Composite of two bright-field transmission electron micrographs (Fig. 6) of polycrystalline Fe-12%Al with 60 ppm C, deformed by 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature, comparing (a) quenched and (b) furnace-cooled material treated at 1100 °C. Both panels carry a 0.4 µm scale bar in the lower right corner and a rotated, only partially readable instrument-data strip along the right edge (mirrored magnification/annotation text). Panel (a), unlabelled, shows an inhomogeneous dislocation substructure: dense dark glide bands of tangled dislocations crossing the field roughly vertically and diagonally, separated by lighter regions containing isolated long straight dislocations. Panel (b), labelled "b)", shows instead a well-developed dislocation cell structure: thick dark cell walls of high dislocation density enclosing lighter, nearly dislocation-free cell interiors whose dimensions are comparable to or smaller than the 0.4 µm scale bar; ordered glide bands are not resolved. Taken together, the two panels demonstrate that the furnace-cooled alloy attains sufficient dislocation mobility to form cells, whereas the quenched alloy deforms by planar glide with tangles only — the microstructural basis for the weak quench effect reported for Fe-12%Al. No numeric values other than the scale bar are printed in either panel.

observations.observation: Both panels are bright-field TEM micrographs and each contains a 0.4 µm scale bar in the lower right corner.
Panel (a) shows dense dark bands of tangled dislocations separated by lighter areas traversed by individual long straight dislocations, i.e. glide-band/tangle structure rather than cells.
Panel (b) shows a dislocation cell structure with thick dark cell walls and lighter, nearly dislocation-free cell interiors, with cell dimensions of the order of the 0.4 µm scale bar or smaller.
Panel (b) is labelled "b)" at its upper left; panel (a) carries no visible panel letter.
Both panels have a rotated/mirrored instrument-data strip along the right edge whose text is only partially readable at the supplied resolution.
The caption states the material is polycrystalline Fe-12%Al (with 60 ppm C) quenched (a) and furnace cooled (b) from 1100 °C, then given 5.5% compressive straining at 10^-4 s^-1 at room temperature.
The caption states the panels show transmission-electron micrographs of the dislocation distributions.
The citing text states that glide bands with dislocation tangles between them were observed after deformation of the quenched alloy (Fig. 6(a)).
The citing text states that deformation of the furnace-cooled alloy initiated cell formation (Fig. 6(b)).
The citing text states that before deformation only few straight dislocations were present in the quenched alloy, whereas nearly no dislocations were observed in the furnace-cooled alloy.

The citing text states that cell formation requires sufficient dislocation mobility, so the cells seen in (b) but not (a) indicate lower dislocation mobility in the quenched Fe-12%Al alloy, attributed to quenched-in excess vacancies.
The citing text states that the Fe-12%Al alloy with 60 ppm C showed only a weak effect of quenching.

subfigures.description: Bright-field TEM micrograph of the quenched Fe-12%Al (60 ppm C) alloy after 5.5% compression: dark, dense glide bands of heavily tangled dislocations running through the field, separated by lighter regions in which individual straight dislocations are visible. 0.4 µm scale bar at lower right; panel unlabelled.

Bright-field TEM micrograph of the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al (60 ppm C) alloy after 5.5% compression: a dislocation cell structure with thick dark cell walls enclosing lighter, nearly dislocation-free cell interiors. Labelled "b)" at upper left; 0.4 µm scale bar at lower right.
